title: Following a scholar
hookLine: most people follow a qualified scholar or school

lines: A MISSED FAST, MADE UP HOW?
ASK, IF YOU DO NOT KNOW.
cards: Who taught you how to tie your shoes? Not a theory of knots. A person, who knew, and showed you, and you trusted them.
Now a harder question. A Muslim misses a day of the Ramadan fast while traveling. How exactly is it made up, and by when?
A mujtahid can work that out from the sources. But what about the nurse, the bus driver, the student, who has never studied legal theory and never will?
The Qur'an, in Surah al-Nahl, tells its hearers to ask the people of the reminder if they do not know. Today's word is what happens next.

teach.b: The word is taqlid, following: taking a ruling from a qualified scholar without working out the evidence yourself.
Some teachers explain it with a picture from the word's root, a qiladah, a necklace or collar: the follower places the question around the scholar's neck, and the scholar carries the answer.
In Sunni communities, taqlid means following a school: the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i or the Hanbali.

A family in one region may pray by Hanafi rulings because their teachers did, and a family in another by Shafi'i ones. In Shia communities, believers follow a living jurist, called a marja' al-taqlid, a source to follow.
A marja' publishes a book of practical rulings, and a believer can open it and look up the missed fast, the travel prayer, the question about work. Both communities draw a line around it.

Taqlid is for the practical rulings. Jurists in both communities have taught that the core beliefs, God's oneness, the prophethood, are a matter of a person's own understanding, not borrowed. And taqlid has its critics.
Some Sunni voices urge believers to follow the evidence directly rather than a school, and others reply that knowing the evidence well is exactly what the schools were built for.

teach.h: SHIA: A LIVING SOURCE TO FOLLOW.
teach.b: The debate is old and still going.

What taqlid isn't is laziness. It's the same trust as the shoelaces, placed carefully: in someone qualified, someone trustworthy, someone whose method is known. The question a follower asks isn't whether to trust.

how: Sunni Muslims may follow one of the established schools of law, often the one their teachers or region follow; Shia Muslims follow a living marja' al-taqlid and consult that jurist's book of practical rulings.

o: copying whatever the crowd around you happens to do
taking a practical ruling from a qualified scholar or school
accepting core beliefs on someone else's word alone

games.q: following a scholar — tap the pairs.
p: ask, if you do not know

s: taqlid applies to the core beliefs too
jurists in both communities say taqlid is for practical rulings; core beliefs rest on a person's own understanding.
Shia Muslims follow a living jurist for practical rulings
a marja' al-taqlid, who publishes a book of practical rulings.
every Sunni voice agrees on following a school

games.q: you missed a fast while traveling, and you've never studied legal theory. how does the tradition expect you to find the answer?
o: work it out from the Qur'an and hadith alone.
follow a qualified scholar or school.
games.why: ask the people of the reminder if you do not know: in Sunni communities, a school; in Shia communities, a living marja'.

practice: If you're Muslim, ask yourself who taught you to pray and whom they learned from; if you know your school or your marja', say the name quietly and remember one ruling you keep because of them.
If you're not Muslim, ask whose guidance you follow on the things you haven't studied, and why you trust them. Then hold one teacher's face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Taqlid. Following: taking a practical ruling from a qualified scholar or school. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: following, imitation; linked by teachers to qiladah, a necklace or collar.

carryVoice: Your line: follow one who knows. Trust, placed carefully, in someone qualified. Until tomorrow.
